newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rules out Albania force for now.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rules out Albania force for now.

text.p: The United States said on Saturday it was not ready to join a proposed stabilisation force in Albania.
A formal written statement by State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns seemed to leave the door open for pursuing that option at a later date.
Other U.S. officials stressed the difficulty of "occupying" Albania, which plummeted into anarchy after financial "pyramid" schemes collapsed, provoking anti-government outrage and unrest.
Ambassadors of Europe's top security body agreed on Saturday to give broad support to sending foreign troops to Albania to halt anarchy in the Balkan state.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) backed a proposal by the OSCE's mediator in Albania, Franz Vranitzky, to ask foreign governments to send forces, but no individual state gave an explicit commitment to do so.

Referring to Vranitzky's "stabilization" force proposal, Burns said: "We are prepared to study any specific proposal; however, we have not agreed to participate in a stabilisation force at this time."
The senior U.S. official who spoke on condition of anonymity said: "There's been no decision that a military force is appropriate and no planning for a military force."
"To say you are going to occupy the country doesn't make sense," he said.
The official noted that Vranitzky had "established a really good start" in his efforts to forge a political solution to Albania's crisis and emphasised U.S. plans to continue backing that effort.
Vranitzky held talks aboard an Italian frigate in the Adriatic on Friday with leaders of the Albanian government and rebel forces from towns in the south.
The former Austrian chancellor said he was told by the government it could no longer control the armed rebellion and wanted outside intervention to restore order.
"There is no alternative (to foreign intervention) as far as I can see," Vranitzky said on Friday.
The senior U.S. official who spoke to reporters anonymously said Washington thought the credibility of Albanian President Sali Berisha was "quite weak."
But he said "we are not demanding that he leaves ... It depends on what everyone (at the OSCE) thinks."

After weeks of anarchy following the collapse of shady investment schemes in which thousands of Albanians lost their savings, Berisha came under international pressure to quit, a key demand of rebels in the south.

Italy, Albania's biggest economic partner and a leading player in international efforts to halt the country's slide into chaos, signalled that Berisha was no longer a key player and his fate was in the hands of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen also said Berisha should resign.
But in a statement in Tirana quoted by Albanian state television, Berisha said he had no intention of resigning.
In his statement, Burns said all Americans who sought evacuation from Albania and were able to reach the U.S. Embassy in Tirana had been airlifted out of the country.
He said 727 people had been evacuated from Albania by the United States since Thursday, including 319 people as of 2:30 p.m. (1930 GMT) on Saturday.

"All American citizens who requested evacuation and have been able to make their way to our embassy in Tirana have been evacuated," Burns said, adding: "We are offering assistance to foreign nationals on a space-available basis. Many of those who left today were foreign nationals."
Burns and other U.S. officials said the situation in Albania seemed to have improve somewhat on Saturday.
